'''Kathryn Ann Moler''' (born {{abbr|c.|circa}} 1966) is an American [[physicist]], and current dean of research at [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.stanford.edu/2018/05/29/materials-physicist-kathryn-moler-named-stanford-vice-provost-dean-research/|title=Materials physicist Kathryn Moler named Stanford vice provost and dean of research {{!}} Stanford News|last=University|first=Stanford|date=2018-05-29|work=Stanford News|access-date=2018-09-11|language=en-US}}</ref> She received her [[BSc]] (1988) and [[Ph.D.]] (1995) from [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aapt.org/aboutaapt/richtmyeraward_pr20100924.cfm |title=Kathy Moler Selected for 2010 Richtmyer Award |publisher=AAPT.org |date=2013-01-22 |access-date=2013-01-29}}</ref>  After working as a visiting scientist at [[IBM]] [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center|T.J. Watson Research Center]] in 1995, she held a postdoctoral position at [[Princeton University]] from 1995 to 1998. She joined the faculty of Stanford University in 1998, and became an Associate in [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research|CIFAR]]'s Superconductivity Program (now called the Quantum Materials Program) in 2000. She became an [[associate professor]] (with tenure) at Stanford in 2002 and is currently a professor of applied physics and of Physics at Stanford. She currently works in the [[Geballe Laboratory for Advanced Materials]] (GLAM),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stanford.edu/group/glam/ |title=Welcome to the Geballe Laboratory |publisher=Stanford.edu |date=1999-09-01 |access-date=2013-01-29}}</ref> and is the director of the [[Center for Probing the Nanoscale]] (CPN),<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.stanford.edu/group/cpn/ |title=Stanford Center for Probing the Nanoscale |publisher=Stanford.edu |date= |access-date=2013-01-29 |archive-date=2013-03-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130326051809/http://www.stanford.edu/group/cpn/ }}</ref> a National Science Foundation-funded center where Stanford and IBM scientists continue to improve scanning probe methods for measuring, imaging, and controlling [[Nanoscopic scale|nanoscale]] phenomena.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vincentcaprio.org/2010/01 |title=Vincent Caprio's blog » 2010 » January |publisher=Vincentcaprio.org |date= |access-date=2013-01-29}}</ref> She lists her scientific interests and main areas of research and experimentation as:

* Single vortex dynamics in classical and high temperature superconductors,
* Spontaneous currents and vortex effects in highly correlated electron systems, and 
* [[Mesoscopic]] [[superconductors]] and currents in normal metal rings, with an increasing interest in the spin properties of such small structures.

==Career==

Early in her career, with [[John R. Kirtley|John Kirtley]] from IBM, their research demonstrated that one of the predictions of a popular theory for [[high-temperature superconductivity]] was inaccurate by a factor of 10.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.sunysb.edu/posterproject/biographies/moler.html |title=Poster Project, Biographies, Moler |publisher=Math.sunysb.edu |date= |access-date=2013-01-29}}</ref> In 2011 her research group placed two non-magnetic materials (complex oxides) together and discovered an unexpected result: The layer where the two materials meet has both magnetic and superconducting regions. These are two properties that are normally incompatible, since "superconducting materials, which conduct electricity with no resistance and 100 percent efficiency, normally expel any magnetic field that comes near them."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ornl.gov/info/news/pulse/no346/story3.shtml |title=DOE Pulse |publisher=Ornl.gov |date=2011-09-19 |access-date=2013-01-29}}</ref>  Exploration of this phenomenon will be aimed toward discovery of whether the properties co-exist uneasily, or this marks the discovery of an exotic new form of superconductivity that actively interacts with magnetism.

In May 2018, Moler was named vice provost and dean of research at Stanford University, effective September 1, 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.stanford.edu/2018/05/29/materials-physicist-kathryn-moler-named-stanford-vice-provost-dean-research/|title=Materials physicist Kathryn Moler named Stanford vice provost and dean of research {{!}} Stanford News|last=University|first=Stanford|date=2018-05-29|work=Stanford News|access-date=2018-09-11|language=en-US}}</ref>
